title: Statistical Methods - Reading Graphs
introductionText:
Term 3 · Statistics
Statistical Methods — Reading Graphs
The Big Idea: Graphs answer questions: which is the most, which is the least, how many
more, and how many altogether.
Say It Like This
Read aloud
"Look at this graph of how children came to school. Every block is one child. Which column
is tallest? Walk — so most children walked. How many more walked than came by car?
Count the walk blocks that stick up above the car column: 1, 2, 3. Three more. To find how
many children altogether, add all the columns."
Watch Out For
The slip almost every child makes
"How many more" answered with the bigger number. Same slip as in Unit 2. Put a ruler
across the top of the shorter column and count only the blocks above it.
Forgetting to read the labels. Before any question, read the title and the words under
each column together.
Try It at Home
Game 1 — Balcony car count (10 minutes)
From a window or balcony, count the colours of cars going past for 5 minutes. Build a
block graph with Lego — one brick for each car, a tower for each colour. Ask: which colour
won? How many more white than red?
Game 2 — Weather week (a week)
Each day, draw the weather in a pictogram: a sun, a cloud or a wind swirl. At the end of
the week ask three questions about it — and let him ask you one.

Count each column with him, then ask him to make up a question about the graph for you to answer.
More examples to talk about
• 6 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 15 children altogether.
• A column with no blocks means zero — nobody chose it.
• Every graph needs a title, or nobody knows what it's about.
• A pictogram and a block graph can show exactly the same numbers.
• Tricky: bus and bike together (6) are the same as walk (6).
Key Words
block graph pictogram column title most least total how many more
